title: After a Team Defeat, Be a First Responder
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author argues that after a setback the best leaders act as first responders, not cheerleaders. What the team needs first is the leader's presence and a willing ear, not optimism, wisdom or blame. Body language and facial expression must carry no hint of disappointment or disgust during the few minutes it takes teams to regain their equilibrium. Only then should positivity, lessons and coaching flow. The move is sequencing: respond first, coach second, and never skip the responding part.
points: After a defeat, a leader's presence matters more than words.
Adding value too soon impedes recovery, so leaders should resist pep talks until people can hear them.
Body language and facial expression must show no disappointment or disgust.
Recovery usually takes minutes, after which lessons and optimism can be shared.
quotes: In the case of a team mishap or defeat, the care most required is simply the presence of the leader and a willing ear. Anything more, and a leader actually impedes recovery, not aids it.
Leaders who don’t quickly arrive at the scene and offer the support of their presence miss the boat. They don’t need to offer optimism or words of wisdom. They simply need to be present.
The team is not yet ready for words or explanations or cheerleading. They need to get past the disappointment or disillusionment of the negative outcome.
Once the team recovers their equilibrium, it is time for positivity and optimism to flow from the leader. Valuable lessons and insights can now be shared.

The best leaders are first responders and then masterful coaches. They don’t skip the responder part. Show up physically as soon as you can, but don’t say much until people are ready. You’ll know when.
